\chapter{Around The Room}
\label{ch:la-caja-y-la-lampara}
\hlchaptermodality{366}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say la caja, la lámpara, la almohada, la escalera and el armario, and name the furniture of an ordinary room.}

Complete ES-C366-armario: name five things in a room, and say what each of them holds or does.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[la caja]{la caja — the box that became the cash}

\label{lesson:ES-C366-caja}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{short}, then \emph{full}. (\emph{Corto}; \emph{lleno}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la casa — the word \emph{caja} is constantly mistaken for, and is not related to.
  \item la bolsa — the other thing you carry things in, so the pair sits together.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{KA-ha}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{j} is the jota, scraped at the back of the throat, and the \emph{c} is a hard \emph{k}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la caja} — \textquotedblleft{}the box.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{capsa} was a box, and in particular the cylindrical case a Roman kept scrolls in. English holds it as \textbf{case} in the container sense; as \textbf{capsule}, which is \emph{capsula}, a little \emph{capsa}; and, arriving through French \emph{châssis}, as \textbf{chassis}, the frame a car is built onto.

The route into Spanish deserves a hedge. The \emph{-ps-} in the middle of \emph{capsa} softens into a \emph{sh}-like sound in Catalan and in Occitan, which is how Catalan arrives at \emph{caixa}, and it does not behave that way in Castilian left to itself. So \emph{caja} most likely walked in from the east rather than being inherited straight down the line. The usual account says Catalan or Occitan carried it.

The reward for all this is \textbf{cash}. English took \emph{cash} from French \emph{casse} or Italian \emph{cassa}, and for its first stretch of life the English word meant \textbf{the money box} — not the money. Only later did the contents take the name of the container. A \textbf{cashier} is still the person who minds that box.

Be careful with the other \emph{cashier}, though: the verb, \textquotedblleft{}to dismiss an officer from service.\textquotedblright{} That one came from French \emph{casser}, \textquotedblleft{}to break, to annul\textquotedblright{}, and is not related to the box at all. Two spellings alike, two histories.

And \textbf{caja} is no relative of \emph{casa}. Latin \emph{casa} was a hut; it pushed the grander \emph{domus} out of everyday Latin, and it gave English \textbf{casino}, \textquotedblleft{}a little house.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now name a container and say what state it is in: \emph{la caja está llena}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la caja}
  \item \emph{una caja}
  \item \emph{la caja está llena}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did a Latin \emph{capsa} hold? (Scrolls.) And what did English \emph{cash} mean first? (The box, not the money in it.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la lámpara]{la lámpara — the shining thing with a letter swapped}

\label{lesson:ES-C366-lampara}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{full}, then \emph{the box}. (\emph{Lleno}; \emph{la caja}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la luz — the light itself, before the thing that holds it.
  \item la noche — when a \emph{lámpara} earns its keep.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{LAM-pa-ra}, three beats with the weight on the first — the written accent is there to tell you so. Both \emph{r} sounds are single taps. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la lámpara} — \textquotedblleft{}the lamp.\textquotedblright{}

Greek \textbf{lampein} meant to shine. From it came \textbf{lampas}, a torch — light you could carry with you. Latin borrowed the Greek word as \emph{lampada}, and Spanish took it over from Latin.

But listen to what Spanish says now: \emph{LAM-pa-ra}, with an \emph{r} in it. Older Spanish really did say \emph{lámpada}, and the \emph{r} is a repair. The word held two very similar beats sitting close together, and the language traded the second of them for a different sound rather than keep saying both. The \emph{r} in \emph{lámpara} is a substitution, not an inheritance — a small scar you can hear.

English has the family through French. A \textbf{lamp} is Old French \emph{lampe}, the same torch. A \textbf{lantern} is the Greek \emph{lampter}, a light-holder, which picked up an intrusive \emph{n} passing through Latin and has kept it ever since.

The real prize, though, is elsewhere in Spanish. \textbf{Relámpago} — lightning — is this root with a prefix on the front: the shining that flashes back out of a cloud. The verb \emph{relampaguear} is what a storm does. Learn the lamp and you have quietly learned the lightning as well.

One word does not belong here, however much it wants to. \textbf{Lampoon} is French \emph{lampons}, \textquotedblleft{}let us drink\textquotedblright{}, the refrain shouted in old drinking songs. It reached English satire by an entirely separate road, and it is exactly the kind of lookalike that sneaks into a family it has no claim on.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now name the thing that makes light indoors, and hear its root again in \emph{relámpago}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la lámpara}
  \item \emph{una lámpara}
  \item \emph{la lámpara de la casa}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Greek \emph{lampein} mean? (To shine.) And why does \emph{lámpara} carry an \emph{r} where older Spanish had a \emph{d}? (Two like sounds sat too close, so one was traded away.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la almohada]{la almohada — the Arabic word for your cheek}

\label{lesson:ES-C366-almohada}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the box}, then \emph{the lamp}. (\emph{La caja}; \emph{la lámpara}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la cama — the \emph{almohada} lives on it.
  \item el sueño — what the pillow is for.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{al-mo-A-da}, four beats with the weight on the third. The \emph{h} is silent, doing nothing at all, the way it does nothing in \emph{hermano}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la almohada} — \textquotedblleft{}the pillow.\textquotedblright{}

Spanish took this word from Arabic, and it took the Arabic article along with it. Andalusi Arabic \textbf{al-mukhadda} came over whole — \emph{al-} means \textquotedblleft{}the\textquotedblright{} — and Spanish never pried the article off. The same fused \emph{al-} sits at the front of \emph{alcalde}, \emph{alcohol}, \emph{algodón} and \emph{almacén}. When you say \emph{la almohada} you are saying \textquotedblleft{}the\textquotedblright{} twice, once in each language, and nobody minds.

Underneath the article is \textbf{khadd}, \textquotedblleft{}cheek.\textquotedblright{} The \emph{mi-} on the front is the Arabic shape that builds a noun for the tool that does something: \emph{fataha} is \textquotedblleft{}to open\textquotedblright{}, and \emph{miftah} is \textquotedblleft{}a key.\textquotedblright{} So \emph{al-mukhadda} is the cheek-instrument. The thing your cheek goes on.

Now the strange part, and the honest one. This word has \textbf{no English relative whatever}. Not a borrowed one, not an inherited one, not even a learned one lurking in a medical dictionary. English \emph{pillow} comes down from Latin \emph{pulvīnus} through Old English, and \emph{cushion} from a Vulgar Latin \emph{coxīnum}. There is nowhere in your English memory to hang \emph{almohada}, which means you get to learn it the plain way: by putting your cheek on it. That happens rarely enough to be worth noticing when it does.

A small note on the article. Learners who have met \emph{el agua} sometimes reach for \emph{el} here. \emph{Agua} takes \emph{el} because its opening \emph{a} is the stressed one; \emph{almohada} carries its weight on \emph{-ha-}, and stays \textbf{la almohada}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now furnish a bed in Spanish, with a word that came from Arabic and kept its article.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la almohada}
  \item \emph{una almohada}
  \item \emph{la almohada de la cama}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the \emph{al-} at the front of \emph{almohada} mean? (The — it is the Arabic article.) And what is the word underneath it? (\emph{Khadd}, cheek: the cheek-instrument.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la escalera]{la escalera — the ladder that grew a vowel}

\label{lesson:ES-C366-escalera}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the lamp}, then \emph{the pillow}. (\emph{La lámpara}; \emph{la almohada}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el piso — the \emph{escalera} is what joins one \emph{piso} to the next.
  \item la escuela — another Spanish word that grew the same opening \emph{e}.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{es-ka-LE-ra}, four beats with the weight on the third. The \emph{r} is a single tap, never rolled, and the opening \emph{es-} is unhurried. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la escalera} — \textquotedblleft{}the stairs, the ladder.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{scāla} was a ladder or a flight of steps, and \emph{scālāria} was the whole staircase. Spanish inherited it — but listen to the front of the Spanish word. Latin opened with \emph{sc-}. Spanish opens with \emph{es-}. A vowel grew there, the same way it grew in \emph{escuela} from \emph{schola}, in \emph{estrella} from \emph{stella}, and in \emph{espada} from \emph{spatha}. Say those three aloud in a row and you can hear Spanish doing the same thing each time it met that opening.

English has the climbing half of the family. To \textbf{scale} a wall is to set a \emph{scāla} against it. \textbf{Ascend}, \textbf{descend} and \textbf{transcend} come from \emph{scandere}, \textquotedblleft{}to climb\textquotedblright{}, the verb the ladder-word is built on. And \textbf{echelon} is French \emph{échelon}, a rung of a ladder — which is why an echelon of an army, or of a company, is a step that somebody is standing on above you.

One relative has to be handed over carefully. \textbf{Escalate} is not an old descendant of \emph{scāla}. It is a twentieth-century back-formation from \textbf{escalator}, and \emph{escalator} was a trademark, registered by the Otis company in 1900 and built to sound Latin. So a conflict that escalates is climbing a machine that a marketing department named.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now name the way from one floor to the next: \emph{la escalera}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la escalera}
  \item \emph{una escalera}
  \item \emph{la escalera del piso}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was a Latin \emph{scāla}? (A ladder or flight of steps.) And where does English \emph{escalate} really come from? (From \emph{escalator}, an Otis trademark of 1900.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el armario]{el armario — where the gear was kept}

\label{lesson:ES-C366-armario}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the pillow}, then \emph{the stairs}. (\emph{La almohada}; \emph{la escalera}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la ropa — what an \emph{armario} is full of.
  \item la habitación — the room the \emph{armario} stands in.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ar-MA-rio}, three beats with the weight on the second. Both \emph{r} sounds are single taps, and the \emph{-rio} runs together into one beat. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el armario} — \textquotedblleft{}the wardrobe, the cupboard.\textquotedblright{}

Start with the question the word invites: why does a place for keeping clothes begin like \emph{arms}? Because Latin \textbf{arma} did not mean weapons. It meant \textbf{tools, equipment, gear} — whatever a person needed on hand to do a job. An \textbf{armārium} was therefore the place where your gear lived: a chest, a cupboard, a recess fitted into a wall. Monastic libraries had one for their books.

The fighting sense came afterwards, and English mostly inherited that half: \textbf{arms} in the military sense, \textbf{army} from \emph{armāta}, \textbf{armour} from \emph{armātūra}.

The best of the family is \textbf{alarm}. Italians shouted \emph{all'arme!} — \textquotedblleft{}to the arms!\textquotedblright{} — and French and then English borrowed the entire shouted phrase and froze it into a noun. So an alarm clock is a small machine yelling \textquotedblleft{}to arms!\textquotedblright{} at you before dawn. Spanish has \emph{alarma} from the same cry.

That same Latin \emph{armārium} also went through French as \emph{armoire}, and English borrowed that too. \textbf{Armario} and \textbf{armoire} are one Latin word that reached English by a different door than the one it took into Spanish.

Two neighbours, sorted out. \textbf{Armonía}, harmony, is Greek \emph{harmonia}, and it genuinely is a distant relative of \emph{arma} — both go back to an old root for fitting things together. \textbf{Farmacia} is Greek \emph{pharmakon}, a drug, and it is not related at all. The one that looks unrelated is; the one that looks related is not.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now say where your clothes live: \emph{la ropa está en el armario}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el armario}
  \item \emph{un armario}
  \item \emph{la ropa está en el armario}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Latin \emph{arma} mean? (Tools and gear, not weapons.) And what is an \emph{alarm} taken literally? (Italian \emph{all'arme} — to the arms!)
\end{tcolorbox}
